entries.771cf3561490fc00c17e98bc73850108071675fb: <div sID="gen11714" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="70" osisID="Ps.70" sID="Ps.70"/> <div eID="gen11714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11715" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11716" type="x-p"/> This psalm is adapted to a state of affliction; it is copied almost word for word from the fortieth, and, some think for that reason, is entitled, "a psalm to bring to remembrance;" for it may be of use sometimes to pray over the prayers we have formerly made to God upon similar occasions, which may be done with new affections. David here prays that God would send, I. Help to himself, <reference osisRef="Ps.70.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.70.5">5</reference>. II. Shame to his enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.70.2-Ps.70.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. III. Joy to his friends, <reference osisRef="Ps.70.4">ver. 4</reference>. These five verses were the <reference osisRef="Ps.40.13-Ps.40.17 Ps.70.1-Ps.70.5">last five verses of Ps. xl.</reference> He seems to have intended this short prayer to be both for himself and us a salve for every sore, and therefore to be always in mind; and in singing we may apply it to our particular troubles, whatever they are.
entries.73c773a2c2bce1d66daa97f0f180b5baa70357b4: <div eID="gen11716" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11715" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Urgent Petitions.</title> <div sID="gen11717" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="italic">Make haste,</hi> O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> Let them be ashamed and confounded that seek after my soul: let them be turned backward, and put to confusion, that desire my hurt. 3 Let them be turned back for a reward of their shame that say, Aha, aha. <hi type="super">4</hi> Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: and let such as love thy salvation say continually, Let God be magnified. <hi type="super">5</hi> But I <hi type="italic">am</hi> poor and needy: make haste unto me, O God: thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my help and my deliverer; <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , make no tarrying. <div eID="gen11717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11718" type="x-p"/> The title tells us that this psalm was designed to bring to remembrance; that is, to put God in remembrance of his mercy and promises (for so we are said to do when we pray to him and plead with him. <reference osisRef="Isa.43.26">Isa. xliii. 26</reference>, <hi type="italic">Put me in remembrance</hi>)—not that the Eternal Mind needs a remembrancer, but this honour he is pleased to put upon the prayer of faith. Or, rather, to put himself and others in remembrance of former afflictions, that we may never be secure, but always in expectation of troubles, and of former devotions, that when the clouds return after the rain we may have recourse to the same means which we have formerly found effectual for fetching in comfort and relief. We may in prayer use the words we have often used before: our Saviour in his agony prayed thrice, saying the same words; so David here uses the words he had used before, yet not without some alterations, to show that he did not design to tie himself or others to them as a form. God looks at the heart, not at the words. <div eID="gen11718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11719" type="x-p"/> I. David here prays that God would make haste to relieve and succour him (<reference osisRef="Ps.70.1">v. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.70.5">5</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am poor and needy,</hi> in want and distress, and much at a loss within myself. Poverty and necessity are very good pleas in prayer to a God of infinite mercy, who despises not the sighing of a contrite heart, who has pronounced a blessing upon the poor in spirit, and who fills the hungry with good things. He prays, 1. That God would appear for him to deliver him from his troubles in due time. 2. That in the mean time he would come in to his aid, to help him under his troubles, that he might not sink and faint. 3. That he would do this quickly: <hi type="italic">Make haste</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.70.1">v. 1</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="Ps.70.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Make haste, make no tarrying.</hi> Sometimes God seems to delay helping his own people, that he may excite such earnest desires as these. <hi type="italic">He that believes does not make haste,</hi> so as to anticipate or outrun the divine counsels, so as to force a way of escape or to take any unlawful methods of relief; but he may make haste by going forth to meet God in humble prayer that he would hasten the desired succour. "<hi type="italic">Make haste unto me,</hi> for the longing desire of my soul is towards thee; I shall perish if I be not speedily helped. I have no other to expect relief from: <hi type="italic">Thou art my help and my delivered.</hi> Thou hast engaged to be so to all that seek thee; I depend upon thee to be so to me; I have often found thee so; and thou art sufficient, all-sufficient, to be so; therefore make haste to me." <div eID="gen11719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11720" type="x-p"/> II. He prays that God would fill the faces of his enemies with shame, <reference osisRef="Ps.70.2-Ps.70.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. Observe, 1. How he describes them; they sought after his soul—his life, to destroy that—his mind, to disturb that, to draw him from God to sin and to despair. They desired his hurt, his ruin; when any calamity befel him or threatened him they said, "<hi type="italic">Aha, aha! so would we have it;</hi> we shall gain our point now, and see him ruined." Thus spiteful, thus insolent, were they. 2. What his prayer is against them: "<hi type="italic">Let them be ashamed;</hi> let them be brought to repentance, so filled with shame as that they may seek thy name (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.16">Ps. lxxxiii. 16</reference>); let them see their fault and folly in fighting against those whom thou dost protect, and be <hi type="italic">ashamed of their envy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa. xxvi. 11</reference>. However, let their designs against me be frustrated and their measures broken; let them be turned back from their malicious pursuits, and then they will be ashamed and confounded, and, like the enemies of the Jews, <hi type="italic">much cast down in their own eyes,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Gen.6.16">Gen. vi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen11720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11721" type="x-p"/> III. He prays that God would fill the hearts of his friends with joy (<reference osisRef="Ps.70.4">v. 4</reference>), that all those who seek God and love his salvation, who desire it, delight in it, and depend upon it, may have continual matter for joy and praise and hearts for both; and then he doubts not but that he should put in for a share of the blessing he prays for; and so may we if we answer the character. 1. Let us make the service of God our great business and the favour of God our great delight and pleasure, for that is seeking him and loving his salvation. Let the pursuit of a happiness in God be our great care and the enjoyment of it our great satisfaction. A heart to love the salvation of the Lord, and to prefer it before any secular advantages whatsoever, so as cheerfully to quit all rather than hazard our salvation, is a good evidence of our interest in it and title to it. 2. Let us then be assured that, if it be not our own fault, the joy of the Lord shall fill our minds and the high praises of the Lord shall fill our mouths. Those that seek God, if they seek him early and seek him diligently, shall rejoice and be glad in him, for their seeking him is an evidence of his good-will to them and an earnest of their finding him, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.3">Ps. cv. 3</reference>. There is pleasure and joy even in seeking God, for it is one of the fundamental principles of religion that God is the <hi type="italic">rewarder of all those that diligently seek him.</hi> Those that love God's salvation shall say with pleasure, with constant pleasure (for praising God, if we make it our continual work, will be our continual feast), <hi type="italic">Let God be magnified,</hi> as he will be, to eternity, in the salvation of his people. All who wish well to the comfort of the saints, and to the glory of God, cannot but say a hearty <hi type="italic">amen</hi> to this prayer, that those who love God's salvation may say continually, <hi type="italic">Let God be magnified.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.70"/> <div eID="gen11721" type="x-p"/>

entries.4611dcef38d563165b550d6edbc55516726c8034: <chapter n="70" osisID="Ps.70" sID="Ps.70"/><div eID="gen9600" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6275"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 70</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.70.1-Ps.70.5">Psa 70:1-5</reference>. This corresponds to <reference osisRef="Ps.40.13-Ps.40.17">Psa 40:13-17</reference> with a very few variations, as "turn back" (<reference osisRef="Ps.70.3">Psa 70:3</reference>) for "desolate," and "make haste unto me" (<reference osisRef="Ps.70.5">Psa 70:5</reference>) for "thinketh upon me." It forms a suitable appendix to the preceding, and is called "a Psalm to bring to remembrance," as the thirty-eighth [see on <reference osisRef="Ps.38.1">Psa 38:1</reference>, title].</title> <div sID="gen9601" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.70"/>

entries.854214b55bc6fa246de18c338d5cb14d3fa8d207: <div eID="gen20848" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20849" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20850" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20850" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20849" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20851" type="x-p"/> The psalmist prays for speedy deliverance, <reference osisRef="Psa.70.1">Psa 70:1</reference>; prays against those who sought his life, <reference osisRef="Psa.70.2">Psa 70:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.70.3">Psa 70:3</reference>; and for the blessedness of those who sought God, <reference osisRef="Psa.70.4">Psa 70:4</reference>; urges his speedy deliverance, <reference osisRef="Psa.70.5">Psa 70:5</reference>. <div eID="gen20851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20852" type="x-p"/> The title in the Hebrew is, To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David, to bring to remembranee. There seems little sense in this title. It seems to intimate that the Psalm was written as a memorial that David had been in sore affliction, and that God had delivered him. So the Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic. It is almost word for word the same with the five last verses of Psalm 40, to the notes on which the reader is referred. <div eID="gen20852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20853" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20854" type="x-p"/> Make haste to help me - I am in extreme distress, and the most imminent danger. Haste to help me, or I am lost.
entries.b8dba235c9174237af4d1f58a63769a77191a264: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20855" type="x-p"/> Let them be turned backward - They are coming in a body against me. Lord, stop their progress!
entries.ccf2180418580aa90709e186e671eeb5666173dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20856" type="x-p"/> That say, Aha, aha - האה האה Heach! heach! a note of supreme contempt. See on <reference osisRef="Psa.40.15">Psa 40:15</reference> (note).
entries.cc3998fcc24556a2c8f3acd75610ae3732b74d3b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20857" type="x-p"/> Let God be magnified - Let his glory, mercy, and kindness, continually appear in the increase of his own work in the souls of his followers!
entries.1e385c7c2846eacc7471022b15fbb4d489be1cb1: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20858" type="x-p"/> But I am poor and needy - עני ואביון ani veebyon, I am a poor man, and a beggar - an afflicted beggar; a sense of my poverty causes me to beg. <div eID="gen20858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20859" type="x-p"/> Thou art my help - I know thou hast enough, and to spare; and therefore I come to thee. <div eID="gen20859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20860" type="x-p"/> Make no tarrying - My wants are many, my danger great, my time short. O God, delay not!  <chapter eID="Ps.70"/> <div eID="gen20860" type="x-p"/>

entries.248ed3b294206d63320ad355f07a25dbd7220806: <div eID="gen9705" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Cry of a Persecuted One for Help</title> <div sID="gen9706" type="x-p"/> This short Psalm, placed after Ps 69 on account of the kindred nature of its contents (cf. more especially v. 6 with <reference osisRef="Ps.69.30">Psa 69:30</reference>), is, with but few deviations, a repetition of Psa 40:14. This portion of the second half of Ps 40 is detached from it and converted into the Elohimic style. Concerning להזכּיר, <hi type="italic">at the presentation of the memorial portion of the mincha</hi>, vid., Psa 38:1. It is obvious that David himself is not the author of the Psalm in this stunted form. The לדוד is moreover justified, if he composed the original Psalm which is here modified and appropriated to a special liturgical use. <div eID="gen9706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9707" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.70.1-Ps.70.3">Psa 70:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9708" type="x-p"/> We see at once at the very beginning, in the omission of the רצה (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.14">Psa 40:14</reference>), that what we have here before us is a fragment of Ps 40, and perhaps a fragment that only accidentally came to have an independent existence. The להצּילני, which was under the government of רצה, now belongs to הוּשׁה, and the construction is without example elsewhere. In <reference osisRef="Ps.70.3">Psa 70:3</reference> (= <reference osisRef="Ps.40.15">Psa 40:15</reference>) יחד and לספּותהּ are given up entirely; the original is more full-toned and soaring. Instead of ישׁמּוּ, <hi type="italic">torpescant</hi>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.70.4">Psa 70:4</reference></hi> has ישׁוּבוּ, <hi type="italic">recedant</hi> (as in Ps 6:11, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.9.18">Psa 9:18</reference>), which is all the more flat for coming after יסגו אחור. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.70.4">Psa 70:4</reference></hi>, after ויאמרים the לי, which cannot here (cf. on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.21">Psa 35:21</reference>) be dispensed with, is wanting.
entries.73294e1dfad4600f9cbc8df87dde968aec8a07ec: <reference osisRef="Ps.70.4-Ps.70.5">Psa 70:4-5</reference> ויאמרו instead of יאמרו is unimportant. But since the divine name <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi> is now for once chosen side by side with <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi>, it certainly had a strong claim to be retained in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.70.5">Psa 70:5</reference></hi>. Instead of תּשׁועתך we have ישׁועתך here; instead of עזרתי, here עזרי. And instead of אדני יחשׁב לי we have here אלהים חוּשׁה־לּי - the hope is turned into petition: <hi type="italic">make haste unto me</hi>, is an innovation in expression that is caused by the taking over of the לי.  <chapter eID="Ps.70"/> <div eID="gen9708" type="x-p"/>

entries.1265a1624fde5ee48b100ac3617a997ed9218764:
PSALM 70
This psalm is merely a part of the fortieth, and the inscription, To call to remembrance, is perhaps designed to indicate this; David having taken these five verses out of that other psalm, and accommodated them for being used on some particular occasion. I shall only here repeat the words of the text; and would refer the reader for the interpretation to the proper place.
To the chief musician of David, to call to remembrance.
Psalm 70:1-5
1. O God! make haste to deliver me: O Jehovah! hasten to my help. 2. Let those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded; let those who desire my hurt be turned backward, and put to confusion 3. Let those who say to me, Aha! aha! perish as a reward of their shame. 4. Let all those who seek thee rejoice and exult in thee: let those who love thy salvation say, Let God be magnified for evermore! 5. As for me, I am poor and needy: O God! hasten to me: thou art my help and my deliverer: O Jehovah! make no delay.
